prompt: For a string held at both ends, why must the separation constant K be negative?

choices.text: With K > 0 the solutions are growing and decaying exponentials, which can't be zero at both ends (except the trivial u = 0)
Because the wave equation has no solutions with K > 0
choices.why: It does have solutions with K > 0, sums of exponentials. They just can't meet the string's boundary conditions.

choices.text: Because a negative K makes the string shorter
choices.why: K doesn't change the length L. It decides whether the solutions oscillate or grow and decay.

choices.text: Because K is the square of the speed, and speeds are negative
choices.why: K is not the speed. A negative K is what gives oscillating sine and cosine solutions.

explanation: With K > 0, X(x) is a sum of a growing and a decaying exponential, which can't be zero at both x = 0 and x = L unless it is zero everywhere. With K = −p^2 < 0, the solutions oscillate, and these can fit the boundary conditions.

prompt: What does Euler's formula say e^(iθ) equals?

choices.text: cos θ + i sin θ
cos θ − i sin θ
choices.why: That is e^(−iθ), the formula for the negative exponent.

choices.text: sin θ + i cos θ
choices.why: The cosine is the real part and the sine the imaginary part: e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ.

choices.text: e^(θ) × i
choices.why: Euler's formula turns a complex exponential into cosine and sine.

explanation: Euler's formula is e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ. It turns the complex exponentials Ae^(ipx) + Be^(−ipx) into the oscillating form c1 cos(px) + c2 sin(px).

prompt: The string's spatial solution is X(x) = c1 cos(px) + c2 sin(px). What does the boundary condition X(0) = 0 tell you?

choices.why: At x = 0, sin(0) = 0, so the c2 term is already zero there; this condition can't fix c2.
At x = 0 both cos(0) and sin(0) are fixed numbers, whatever p is, so this condition says nothing about p.

choices.text: X(x) = 0 everywhere
choices.why: It only removes the cosine term. The sine term can still be nonzero.

explanation: X(0) = c1 cos(0) + c2 sin(0) = c1(1) + c2(0) = c1. Setting this equal to 0 gives c1 = 0, so only the sine term is left: X(x) = c2 sin(px).

prompt: With c1 = 0, the other end of the string needs c2 sin(pL) = 0. Ignoring the trivial c2 = 0, what must be true?

choices.text: pL = nπ, where n is a whole number
pL = 0 only
choices.why: sin is zero at every whole-number multiple of π, not only at 0, so pL = nπ.

choices.text: pL = π/2
choices.why: sin(π/2) = 1, not 0, so that would not satisfy the condition.

choices.text: p can be any number at all
choices.why: Only the values that make sin(pL) = 0 are allowed. This is how quantization appears.

explanation: sin is zero at 0, π, 2π, 3π, …, so sin(pL) = 0 needs pL = nπ, that is p = nπ/L. Only these values of p are allowed.

prompt: The allowed solutions are X(x) = c2 sin(nπx/L). Why is n = 0 left out?

choices.text: It gives X(x) = 0 everywhere, the trivial solution with no wave
Because n can only be negative
choices.why: The allowed values used are n = 1, 2, 3, …

choices.text: Because n = 0 would make the string infinitely long
choices.why: n = 0 doesn't change L. It makes sin(0 · x) = 0 everywhere.

choices.text: Because it gives a wave with infinitely many nodes
choices.why: n = 0 gives no wave at all, not one with many nodes.

explanation: With n = 0, X(x) = c2 sin(0) = 0 at every x: the string doesn't move. That trivial solution is ignored, so n = 1, 2, 3, …

prompt: The string's solutions are X(x) = sin(nπx/L), which have wavelength λ = 2L/n. What is the wavelength, in meters, of the n = 3 solution on a string 1.2 m long?
Where is the node in the middle of the string for the n = 2 solution, X(x) = sin(2πx/L)?

choices.text: At x = L/2
At x = L/4
choices.why: sin(2π(L/4)/L) = sin(π/2) = 1, which is a maximum, not a node.

choices.text: At x = L/3
choices.why: sin(2π/3) is not zero, so x = L/3 is not a node.

choices.text: There is no node between the ends for n = 2
choices.why: The n = 1 solution has no node between the ends; n = 2 has one.

explanation: A node is where sin(2πx/L) = 0 between the ends, which means 2πx/L = π, so x = L/2. The middle of the string stays still while its two halves swing in opposite directions.

prompt: The wave ψ1 = sin(c1x + c2t) has velocity dx/dt = −c2/c1 (with c1 and c2 positive). Which way does it move?

choices.text: Toward smaller x (the negative x-direction)
Toward larger x (the positive x-direction)
choices.why: The velocity −c2/c1 is negative. It is ψ2 = sin(c1x − c2t), with velocity +c2/c1, that moves toward larger x.

choices.text: It does not move; it is a standing wave
choices.why: ψ1 has a nonzero velocity, so it travels. A standing wave comes from adding two traveling waves.

choices.text: It moves up and down only
choices.why: Each point does move up and down, but the wave shape itself travels, with velocity −c2/c1.

explanation: A negative velocity means the wave moves toward smaller x. ψ1 = sin(c1x + c2t) travels in the −x direction, and ψ2 = sin(c1x − c2t) in the +x direction, both at speed c2/c1.

prompt: Adding the two traveling waves gives ψ+ = sin(c1x + c2t) + sin(c1x − c2t) = 2 sin(c1x) cos(c2t). What kind of wave is ψ+?

choices.text: A standing wave, with nodes fixed at x = nπ/c1
A faster traveling wave
choices.why: Its shape sin(c1x) stays in place; only its size changes with time, through cos(c2t). Nothing travels.

choices.text: No wave at all, because the two waves cancel
choices.why: They cancel only at the nodes. Elsewhere the string moves up and down.

choices.text: A traveling wave with no nodes
choices.why: sin(c1x) is zero wherever c1x = nπ, at every time, so there are fixed nodes.

explanation: 2 sin(c1x) cos(c2t) is a fixed shape, sin(c1x), whose size rises and falls with cos(c2t). Its nodes, where sin(c1x) = 0, sit still at x = nπ/c1. Two equal waves traveling in opposite directions add up to a standing wave.

prompt: Section 2.3 writes the negative separation constant as K = −p^2. What does d^2X/dx^2 − KX = 0 become?

choices.why: Replacing K with −p^2 turns −KX into +p^2X. The minus-sign version has exponential solutions, not oscillating ones.

choices.text: d^2X/dx^2 + pX = 0
choices.why: K = −p^2, so p enters squared.
p is not zero. Only the sign in front of the X term changes.

explanation: −KX = −(−p^2)X = +p^2X, so the equation becomes d^2X/dx^2 + p^2X = 0. Writing K as −p^2, with p real, is a way of saying K is negative.

prompt: Why do complex numbers appear in the solutions when the separation constant K is negative?

choices.text: The solutions contain √K, which is imaginary when K < 0
The string's displacement itself is an imaginary number
choices.why: The string's displacement is real. The i comes from √K with K < 0, and Euler's formula later turns it into real sines and cosines.

choices.text: The position x becomes negative along the string
choices.why: x runs from 0 to L. The i comes from taking the square root of the negative constant K.

choices.text: The wave speed v becomes an imaginary number
choices.why: v is an ordinary real speed. It is √K that is imaginary when K < 0.

explanation: The K > 0 solutions have e^(±√K x). With K = −p^2, √K = √(−p^2) = ip, so the solutions become e^(ipx) and e^(−ipx).

prompt: Written with complex exponentials, what is the general solution of d^2X/dx^2 + p^2X = 0?

choices.text: X(x) = Ae^(ipx) + Be^(−ipx)
X(x) = Ae^(px) + Be^(−px)
choices.why: Real exponentials solve d^2X/dx^2 − p^2X = 0, the K > 0 case. The plus sign needs an i in the exponent.

choices.text: X(x) = Ae^(ipx) alone
choices.why: A second-order equation has two independent solutions, so e^(−ipx) is needed too.

choices.text: X(x) = Ae^(ipx) × Be^(−ipx)
choices.why: Solutions are combined by adding, not multiplying. This product would just be the constant AB.

explanation: The two solutions are e^(ipx) and e^(−ipx), and the general solution is any combination of them, Ae^(ipx) + Be^(−ipx). Euler's formula then rewrites it with cosines and sines.

prompt: After using Euler's formula, X(x) = (A + B) cos(px) + i(A − B) sin(px). Which new constants does the section define?

choices.text: c1 = A + B and c2 = i(A − B)
c1 = A − B and c2 = A + B
choices.why: c1 multiplies cos(px), and the coefficient of cos(px) is A + B.

choices.text: c1 = A + B and c2 = A − B
choices.why: The i belongs inside c2: c2 = i(A − B), so that X(x) = c1 cos(px) + c2 sin(px).

choices.text: c1 = AB and c2 = iAB
choices.why: The coefficients are a sum and a difference, A + B and i(A − B), not products.

explanation: Renaming the coefficients c1 = A + B and c2 = i(A − B) gives X(x) = c1 cos(px) + c2 sin(px), the same solution written as oscillating functions.

prompt: Why does the section rewrite Ae^(ipx) + Be^(−ipx) as c1 cos(px) + c2 sin(px)?

choices.text: It shows the oscillation and makes the boundary conditions easy
It gives a different solution, with different wavelengths
choices.why: It is the same function written another way, using Euler's formula. Only the names of the constants change.

choices.text: It removes the constant p from the solution entirely
choices.why: p is still there, inside cos(px) and sin(px).

choices.text: It turns the solution into growing and decaying exponentials
choices.why: cos and sin oscillate between −1 and 1. Growing exponentials belong to the K > 0 case.

explanation: Using Euler's formula is just a rewrite. In the cosine and sine form, the wave's oscillation is plain to see, and cos(0) = 1 and sin(0) = 0 make the condition X(0) = 0 easy to apply.

prompt: The far end of the string needs X(L) = c1 cos(pL) + c2 sin(pL) = 0. Why does this become simply c2 sin(pL) = 0?

choices.text: c1 = 0 was already found from X(0) = 0
cos(pL) is always zero, whatever p and L are
choices.why: cos(pL) is not zero in general. The cosine term drops out because its coefficient c1 is already 0.

choices.text: sin(pL) is always equal to 1 at the far end
choices.why: If sin(pL) were 1, the condition would force c2 = 0. The cosine term vanishes because c1 = 0.

choices.text: The string's length L is zero, so pL = 0
choices.why: L is the string's length, not zero. The first boundary condition, giving c1 = 0, removes the cosine term.

explanation: The first boundary condition, X(0) = c1 = 0, already removed the cosine term. So at x = L only c2 sin(pL) = 0 is left, which leads to pL = nπ.

prompt: Why is X(x) = c2 sin(nπx/L) zero at both ends of the string for every n = 1, 2, 3, …?

choices.text: sin(0) = 0 at x = 0, and sin(nπ) = 0 at x = L
c2 = 0 for every one of the allowed solutions
choices.why: c2 is not zero, or there would be no wave. The sine itself is zero at both ends.

choices.text: cos(0) = 0 at x = 0, and cos(nπ) = 0 at x = L
choices.why: cos(0) = 1 and cos(nπ) is 1 or −1. The solution uses sine, and sin(0) = sin(nπ) = 0.

choices.text: n = 0 makes the sine vanish at both of the ends
choices.why: n = 0 makes the sine zero everywhere, the trivial solution, so it is left out. For n = 1, 2, 3, …, sin(nπ) = 0 at x = L.

explanation: At x = 0 the angle is 0, and at x = L it is nπ. Sine is zero at every whole-number multiple of π, so each allowed solution meets both boundary conditions.

prompt: On a string fixed at both ends, what restricts the waves to certain wavelengths only?

choices.text: The boundary conditions: the wave must be zero at both ends
The wave equation alone, before any conditions are applied
choices.why: On its own the equation allows any p. Requiring zero at both ends is what demands pL = nπ.

choices.text: Euler's formula
choices.why: Euler's formula only rewrites the solution with cosines and sines. It doesn't restrict p.

choices.text: The size of the constants A and B
choices.why: A and B set how big the wave is. The allowed wavelengths come from needing zero at both ends.

explanation: Requiring X(0) = 0 and X(L) = 0 forces pL = nπ, so only p = nπ/L is allowed. Satisfying the boundary conditions is what causes this quantization.

prompt: The section writes X(x) = c2 sin(nπx/L) as c2 sin(ωx). What is ω here?

choices.text: nπ/L
nπ
choices.why: x is multiplied by nπ/L, so ω includes the division by L.

choices.text: L/(nπ)
choices.why: That is upside down. sin(nπx/L) means x is multiplied by nπ/L.

choices.text: 2L/n
choices.why: 2L/n is the wavelength. ω is the number that multiplies x inside the sine, nπ/L.

explanation: Comparing c2 sin(nπx/L) with c2 sin(ωx) shows ω = nπ/L, the same as the allowed value p = nπ/L.

prompt: The string's solutions sin(nπx/L) have wavelength λ = 2L/n. What happens to the wavelength as n increases?

choices.text: It gets shorter
It gets longer
choices.why: n is in the denominator of 2L/n, so a larger n gives a smaller λ.

choices.text: It stays equal to L
choices.why: λ depends on n: 2L for n = 1, L for n = 2, 2L/3 for n = 3, and so on.

choices.text: It doubles with each step in n
choices.why: λ = 2L/n falls as n rises. Going from n = 1 to n = 2 halves it.

explanation: λ = 2L/n is inversely proportional to n. The n = 1 solution has the longest wavelength, 2L, and each higher n fits more, shorter waves onto the string.

prompt: Where along the string is the n = 1 solution, X(x) = sin(πx/L), largest?

choices.text: At the middle, x = L/2
At the ends, x = 0 and x = L
choices.why: sin(0) = 0 and sin(π) = 0, so the ends are nodes, not maxima.

choices.text: At x = L/4
choices.why: There the value is sin(π/4) ≈ 0.71, smaller than sin(π/2) = 1 at the middle.

choices.text: It is the same size everywhere
choices.why: sin(πx/L) rises from 0 at one end to 1 at the middle and falls back to 0 at the other end.

explanation: At x = L/2, πx/L = π/2, and sin(π/2) = 1, the largest a sine can be. The n = 1 wave is a single hump with its peak in the middle.

prompt: Where are the nodes between the ends for the n = 3 solution, X(x) = sin(3πx/L)?

choices.text: At x = L/3 and x = 2L/3
At x = L/2 only
choices.why: At x = L/2 the angle is 3π/2 and sin(3π/2) = −1, a point of largest displacement. A single middle node belongs to n = 2.

choices.text: At x = L/4, L/2 and 3L/4
choices.why: Those are the three nodes of n = 4. The n = 3 solution has n − 1 = 2 nodes.

choices.text: There are no nodes between the ends
choices.why: That is the n = 1 solution. For n = 3, sin(3πx/L) = 0 where 3πx/L = π or 2π.

explanation: Nodes between the ends are where 3πx/L = π or 2π, that is x = L/3 and x = 2L/3. That makes n − 1 = 2 nodes, splitting the string into three equal parts.

prompt: In Exercise 2.3.1, how do the wavelengths of ψ1 = sin(c1x + c2t) and ψ2 = sin(c1x − c2t) compare?

choices.text: They are the same, λ = 2π/c1
ψ1's wavelength is twice ψ2's
choices.why: Both have c1 multiplying x, so both have λ = 2π/c1.

choices.text: ψ2's wavelength is negative
choices.why: A wavelength is a length, so it is positive. ψ2 moves the other way, but its λ is the same 2π/c1.

choices.text: They differ, because they depend on c2
choices.why: The wavelength depends only on c1, the number multiplying x. c2 sets how fast the waves move.

explanation: The wavelength is twice the distance between successive nodes, λ = 2π/c1, for both waves. The two waves differ only in direction: ψ1 moves toward −x and ψ2 toward +x, both at speed c2/c1.

prompt: The difference of the two traveling waves is ψ_(−) = 2 cos(c1x) sin(c2t). Where are its nodes, the points that never move?

choices.text: Where cos(c1x) = 0, at c1x = π/2, 3π/2, …
Where sin(c1x) = 0, at c1x = 0, π, 2π, …
choices.why: Those are the nodes of the sum, ψ_(+) = 2 sin(c1x) cos(c2t). For ψ_(−), cos(c1x) = ±1 there, the places of largest motion.

choices.text: At every x, but only at the time t = 0
choices.why: At t = 0 the whole string is flat for an instant, but most points move later. A node stays at zero at all times.

choices.text: Nowhere, because ψ_(−) is a traveling wave
choices.why: ψ_(−) is a fixed shape, cos(c1x), times sin(c2t), so it is a standing wave with fixed nodes.

explanation: ψ_(−) is the shape cos(c1x) with a size that changes as sin(c2t). It is zero at all times wherever cos(c1x) = 0, at c1x = π/2, 3π/2, …, halfway between the nodes of ψ_(+).

prompt: For the standing wave ψ_(−) = 2 cos(c1x) sin(c2t), what does the string look like at the instant t = 0?

choices.text: Flat: ψ_(−) = 0 at every x, because sin(0) = 0
The shape 2 cos(c1x), at its very largest size
choices.why: That happens when sin(c2t) = 1. At t = 0, sin(0) = 0, so the whole wave is zero.

choices.text: Zero only at its nodes, curved everywhere else
choices.why: At t = 0 the time factor sin(c2t) is zero, so every point, not only the nodes, is at zero for that instant.

choices.text: The shape 2 sin(c1x), like the sum ψ_(+)
choices.why: The x part of ψ_(−) is cos(c1x), and at t = 0 it is multiplied by sin(0) = 0 anyway.

explanation: sin(c2 × 0) = 0, so ψ_(−) = 0 everywhere at t = 0: the string passes through flat, then bulges into the cos(c1x) shape. Nodes are different: they stay at zero at all times.

prompt: Use Euler's formula, e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ. What real number is e^(iπ) equal to?
explanation: e^(iπ) = cos π + i sin π = −1 + i(0) = −1.

prompt: Use π = 3.14. The boundary conditions allow only p = nπ/L. What is p for n = 1 on a string 0.5 m long, in m^−1?
The solution X(x) = sin(nπx/L) has n − 1 nodes between the ends of the string. How many nodes between the ends does the n = 4 solution have?
explanation: n − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3 nodes, at x = L/4, L/2 and 3L/4, where 4πx/L = π, 2π and 3π.

prompt: In Exercise 2.3.1, the wavelength is twice the distance between two successive nodes. If successive nodes of a wave are 0.3 m apart, what is its wavelength, in m?
explanation: λ = 2 × (node spacing) = 2 × 0.3 m = 0.6 m. For ψ1 and ψ2 the nodes are π/c1 apart, so λ = 2π/c1.

prompt: The traveling wave ψ2 = sin(c1x − c2t) moves with velocity c2/c1. What is its speed, in m/s, if c1 = 2 m^−1 and c2 = 10 s^−1?
explanation: v = c2/c1 = (10 s^−1)/(2 m^−1) = 5 m/s, toward larger x.
